First, name the real problem in one solution-free sentence: what is actually failing, and for whom? That defines the decision.

02-diagnostic-route.text: Same incident, two engineers: "payments are failing intermittently." The first digs into the code she wrote last week and burns four hours. The second writes three hypotheses, picks the one a 2-minute query could rule out, and crosses off a third of the search space before the first opens a file. One had a route; one had a hunch.

Diagnosis is search through a space of causes, and ambiguous problems have large spaces. The amateur searches where the light is good (the code they own); the senior searches where information is densest per unit of effort. The Route makes that discipline visible — Section 2 of the memo.

02-diagnostic-route.reveal: Not the most likely — the most CHEAPLY DISQUALIFIABLE. A 2-minute test that eliminates half the suspects whatever its result beats an hour confirming your top guess. You are not trying to be right early; you are trying to shrink the space fastest. Often the best first move is a test you expect to PASS, precisely because passing it rules a whole branch out.

## 2. Diagnostic Route
- Hypothesis A (lag): index worker is behind        → kill-test: newest indexed doc vs newest DB write  → cost: cheap
- Hypothesis B (silent-fail): worker crashes on some events → kill-test: worker error-log + dead-letter count → cost: cheap
- Hypothesis C (stale-cache): query layer serves old results → kill-test: bypass cache, re-query primary → cost: mid
- Run order (cheapest disqualifier first): A → B → C
- Stop rule: one branch confirmed by evidence, or 30 min elapsed → decide
steps: Most-likely hypothesis: A real hypothesis, not a shrug: "maybe a config issue" has no kill-test, so it cannot be on the route.
Span layers you do not own: B and C should reach beyond your own code. Bias hides in "it must be my service".
A falsifiable kill-test each: Each test must be able to return "no" and eliminate a branch. A test that can only confirm is theater.
Cost each test: A timestamp compare is minutes; a code-path change is expensive. Cost decides the order, not your favorite suspect.
Cheapest disqualifier first: Order by elimination-per-minute. The first move can cross off a whole branch in one query.
The stop rule: A concrete time or evidence threshold — past it, diagnosis is procrastination with a stack trace.

storyboard.say: It starts with the feared failure — the concrete thing that could be going wrong, like payments failing intermittently.
That fear spawns a short list of ranked hypotheses — plausible causes, not just the code you happen to own.
You order the hypotheses by information per unit of cost, then reach for the single cheapest kill-test first.
If the test comes back no, you eliminate that branch — a two-minute query can cross off a third of the search space.
Eliminate, then loop back to the next cheapest disqualifier — each test must be able to fail, or it teaches you nothing.
The stop rule guards the loop: when the box is hit, you stop diagnosing and decide instead of digging forever.
The hypothesis that survives every cheap kill-test becomes the leading cause — the survivor you act on.

storyboard.say: This is the whole search-lag system in five boxes. Not the ninety-box poster — just what the failure actually touches.
It starts at the client. A request goes to the API gateway, which routes it into the orders service.
Orders does two things: it writes the record to Postgres, and it emits an event to the index worker.

Postgres is the source of truth and stays correct; the stale search index is the blast radius.

## Context
Release v2.4.0, 14:02. Checkout p99 latency 280ms -> 910ms in 8 min. Error rate flat.

## Assumptions
Latency signal is real (cross-checked two sources). No upstream incident open.

## Decision
Rolled back to v2.3.9 at 14:11.

Rejected option — the most convincing line: The credible alternative AND the specific reason it loses (flag not wired for payments). Write this FIRST; it separates a calibrated call from a reflex.
Verification method: Something that could be RUN to confirm the call worked, with the observed result. This is the seed of the Lesson 08 proof.

We declare the incident resolved, page nobody, and the spike returns at the next

cache metrics, and REOPEN the incident instead of closing it.

A — full rollback to v2.3.9
B — feature-flag the new checkout path off
C — leave it up, instrument harder for 10 more minutes

## Real options (each wins under SOME condition)
A — full rollback to v2.3.9
B — feature-flag the new checkout path off
C — leave it up, instrument harder for 10 more minutes

## Binding constraint (what actually decides)
Customer-facing latency event: the cost of being slow now exceeds the cost of
losing the new feature for an hour. Time-to-recover dominates.

## Choice — by the constraint, not a pro/con tally
A: fastest, fully reversible. B: flag not wired for payments (the L06 failure)
-> double-charge risk. C: keeps the pain live. Under time-to-recover, A wins.

## Reversal condition (the specific change that flips it)
Once the payment flag is wired safely AND latency is isolated to a non-payment
path, the same event next quarter flips to B (smaller blast radius, keeps feature).

## Risk if wrong (reuse the L06 injected failure)
If the spike was downstream, A recovers p99 by coincidence -> pair A with the
L06 detection signal: watch the next traffic peak.

storyboard.say: A real tradeoff starts with real options — each alternative has to win under some plausible condition, not just fill a slot.
Those options get tested against the binding constraint: the one or two things — latency, cost, skill, risk, time — that actually decide.
The constraint selects the choice. Name the constraint and you can explain the whole call in a single sentence.
The choice admits a reversal condition: the specific change in the world that would flip it. No reversal means a one-way door or a bluff.
The choice also carries the risk if wrong — the L06 injected failure, now owned as an explicit column, not hidden.
The pro-con tally is the failure mode. It must NOT decide — a scorecard hides the real constraint behind counted bullets.
So when a principal asks what else you considered and what would make you wrong — the constraint, reversal, and risk are your answer.

08-testa-proof.prompt: You changed a config and the bug went away, so you write "fixed and verified." Before reading on — under the Testa discipline, why is "the symptom disappeared" often the WEAKEST proof, not the strongest?
08-testa-proof.reveal: A vanished symptom proves the symptom is gone right now — not that you fixed the cause, and not that it stays gone. The bug could be intermittent (gone by luck of timing), or your change masked it (the cause still lurks), or it depended on load you are not currently generating. The strongest available proof targets the CAUSE and is repeatable: a failing test that now passes (and failed before your fix), a contract check the artifact must satisfy, a load test that reproduces the original condition. "The symptom disappeared" is where proof STARTS, not where it ends. Testa forces the question: what is the strongest evidence this situation actually allows, and did I run THAT?

storyboard.say: When a reviewer says prove it, you climb this ladder from the top. Rung one: an executable test you ran that failed before and passes after.
That is the strongest evidence, so if you have it, name the mode and go straight to calibrated confidence.
Can't run a real test? Only then drop to rung two: a contract or schema check that machine-verifies the shape.
If even a schema won't fit, drop again to rung three: a domain check on accessibility, security, reliability, or eval.
Last resort, when execution is truly impossible, is rung four: a reviewer rubric. It is proof, but the weakest kind.
The rung you reached sets the ceiling. Reaching only the rubric means you lower the confidence score to match.
Reach for the strongest mode the situation allows, name it, and let confidence track the proof, not your mood.

Context:  Conversion is flat; the new flow is 40% less code; load test is incomplete.

# review_rubric.md  (decision-memo review board, 0–100)

Score the artifact, not the author. Each dimension is pass/partial/fail with a hard cap.

1. ARTIFACT EXISTS & IS INSPECTABLE        cap 72 if missing/thin
   - named file, readable by a stranger, not a paragraph of prose
2. FAILURE NAMED & REALISTIC               cap 82 if no real failure mode
   - a production-grade break, not a toy ("it might error")
3. PROOF IS CONCRETE                        cap 78 if proof is an anecdote
   - measurement vs. a control/baseline, reproducible
4. TRADEOFF IS DEFENSIBLE                    cap 86 if self-serving
   - chosen + rejected option + reversal condition + risk-if-wrong
5. REPAIR PATH STATED                        cap 88 if no rollback/repair
   - what flips, at what threshold, and the autopsy that follows
6. TRANSFER CHANGES CONTEXT                  cap 92 if transfer is a restatement
   - same pattern, genuinely different domain/constraints

Pass  = 80+  (all six present, none faked)
Gold  = 94+  (also: reviewer objection answered, repair re-tested)

# engineering_judgment_decision_memo.md

Cache ONLY negative results (failed lookups), 5s TTL; never cache a valid token.

## Rejected
Caching successful auth — a stale "valid" is a security hole; that risk
dominates the latency win.

A user is banned, their session revoked, but a cached "valid" keeps them in

Contract test: revoked sessions are NEVER served from cache.

Any auth-bypass report flips the cache off immediately — no meeting required.

Name the decision · mark assumptions · compare by cost + reversibility ·

User: every logged-in request. Risk if wrong: SECURITY, not latency.
Privacy: auth state now lives in a second place.

storyboard.say: Promotion Friday. Two engineers say the same words: strong judgment under ambiguity. Only one can open a ledger. Watch what that ledger is made of.
It starts with the Claim — you name what you can do as a provable skill, not a vague topic. The claim registers itself in the ledger.
Next the Artifact: the actual inspectable file. It links into the ledger, so the claim points at something real, not a description of it.
Then Proof — the strongest check available — backs the claim, so the file is not just present but shown to actually work.
The fourth part is the Predicted failure: the autopsy you wrote before the outcome, timestamped into the ledger to prove you called the risk early.
Four parts now feed one ledger. Drop any single part and the package weakens — but it is still a package a skeptic can open.
The binding property is inspectable — committed, timestamped, linked. The skeptic checks it with no questions. Drop this and it is not evidence at all.

15-unlock-gate.proof: A completed gate checklist against your packaged evidence, each criterion marked pass or repair, every repair routed to a named action, and a re-check after repair — applied to YOUR artifact, not a hypothetical.
15-unlock-gate.unlock: Every gate criterion is genuinely met by inspectable evidence, OR is honestly marked "repair needed" with the specific fix named. No criterion is waved through on confidence.
15-unlock-gate.outcome: Run an honest unlock gate on your own work: it opens ONLY when the evidence exists, refuses to round a gap up to a pass, and routes every miss to a specific repair before re-checking. Gate yourself the way a reviewer would — and pass or repair honestly.
15-unlock-gate.doNotClaim: Do not claim the gate "passed" because most criteria were green. A gate is not an average — one missing piece of required evidence means the gate is closed. Honest red is worth more than dishonest green, and a gate you game protects nothing.

15-unlock-gate.text: Every real system has a gate: the merge that needs a green CI run, the release that needs sign-off, the deploy that needs the checklist — because "I am pretty sure it is fine" has shipped more outages than any bug. The engineers trusted with production gate themselves HARDER than the reviewer would, catching their own missing evidence first.

This is where the course tightens into a standard. Transfer proved you can decide anywhere; package made the decision inspectable; now the gate decides whether the evidence is actually sufficient — without mercy and without inflation. If the gate opens on confidence, the package was theater.

15-unlock-gate.prompt: A learner reviews their own evidence: "I hit retrieval, the artifact, the explanation, and the transfer — four of five. The proof is a bit thin but the rest is strong, so I will call it a pass." Honest gate?
15-unlock-gate.reveal: No — that is averaging, and a gate does not average. Proof is a REQUIRED criterion, not a weighted one; "a bit thin" on proof means the gate is closed until the proof is real, no matter how strong the other four are. The instinct to round up — "mostly there, so basically passed" — is exactly the instinct an honest gate exists to stop, because it is the same instinct that ships a release with a skipped test. A gate is a conjunction (all required AND-ed), never a sum. One honest red closes it.

15-unlock-gate.intro: Reading a closed gate, line by line. Four passes, one honest red. Watch why "4 of 5" is not 80% open — it is closed.
